title: Friend or careful?
intro: Almost all insects are harmless and many help us. A few can be pests or sting. Let's learn to live alongside all of them, without fear and without wiping them out.

lessons.title: The helpers
lessons.intro: Without insects there would be few fruits, no rich soil and fewer birds. Let's see how they help us.
lessons.closing: They pollinate, recycle, control pests and feed other animals. Insects do much more good than harm!

exercises.prompt: Match each insect with its job.
exercises.explanation: Every insect has a job in nature.

exercises.prompt: What would happen if all insects disappeared?
options: We'd lack fruit and many birds would go hungry
exercises.explanation: Food chains and soil recycling would break down.

exercises.prompt: What does pollinating mean?
options: Carrying pollen from flower to flower so there are fruits and seeds
exercises.explanation: Without pollination, many plants wouldn't make fruit.

exercises.prompt: Tap the insects that pollinate flowers.
exercises.explanation: Bees, butterflies and many flies carry pollen from flower to flower.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Flies and beetles ___ leftovers and turn them into fertilizer.
exercises.explanation: They are nature's recyclers.

lessons.title: Pests and how to control them
lessons.intro: Some insects, when there are huge numbers of them, damage crops or food: they are pests. How do we control them without harming the others?
lessons.closing: Wiping out all insects also kills the ones that help us. Biological control is better: letting their natural enemies do the job.

exercises.prompt: What is a pest?
options: Huge numbers of one kind of insect that damage crops or food
exercises.explanation: A pest outbreak is huge numbers of one kind of insect in the same place.

exercises.prompt: Match each pest with what it does.

pairs.right: Travels in swarms that eat crops

exercises.explanation: They're only pests when there are huge numbers of them.

exercises.prompt: If we spray insecticide all over the garden, what happens?
options: Bees, ladybugs and other helpers die too
exercises.explanation: Poison can't tell the difference: it kills the helpers too.

exercises.prompt: What is biological control?
options: Using the pest's natural enemies, like ladybugs against aphids
exercises.explanation: One ladybug can eat hundreds of aphids.

exercises.prompt: You find weevils in the flour. What's best?
options: Throw that flour away and keep food in tightly closed jars
exercises.explanation: Storing food well prevents pests without poison.

lessons.title: The ones that can sting or spread disease
lessons.intro: A few insects can sting or spread disease, like some mosquitoes and the kissing bug. They aren't evil: they do what they need to live. Let's learn to protect ourselves.
lessons.closing: Staying safe is easy: no standing water, use a mosquito net and long clothes, and tell an adult if something bites you. There's no need to kill every insect.

exercises.prompt: Why does the female mosquito bite?
options: She needs blood to lay her eggs
exercises.explanation: Only females bite. Males drink nectar.

exercises.prompt: Where do mosquitoes lay their eggs?
options: In still water: buckets, tires or vases
exercises.explanation: That's why we empty water that sits still.

exercises.prompt: What helps stop mosquitoes from hatching near your home?
exercises.explanation: Emptying still water: that's where mosquitoes lay their eggs. Without standing water, they can't hatch.

exercises.prompt: A bee stings you and it swells up a lot or it's hard to breathe. What do you do?
options: I tell an adult right away
exercises.explanation: Some people are allergic. Telling an adult is always the right thing.

exercises.prompt: The kissing bug can spread a disease. If you see one at home, what's the safest thing?
options: Don't touch it and tell an adult
exercises.explanation: Look without touching and tell someone: that keeps you safe.

lessons.title: Friend or careful?
lessons.intro: Final review: decide whether each insect is harmless, can be a pest, or needs care because it can sting or spread disease.
lessons.closing: Almost all are harmless. With the rest, you just need to know them and stay safe. You're a forest ranger who looks after insects!

exercises.prompt: Put each insect in its box.
bins: Careful: can sting or spread disease
exercises.explanation: Bees help us enormously, but they can sting if they feel attacked: so, take care.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is harmless?
exercises.explanation: Dragonflies don't sting people and they eat mosquitoes.

exercises.prompt: What does “harmful” mean here?
options: That it can damage crops or food
exercises.explanation: A harmful insect can be a pest, but it isn't evil.

exercises.prompt: Put each insect in its box.
bins: Careful: can sting or spread disease
exercises.explanation: The kissing bug can spread a disease: if you see one at home, tell an adult. Almost all other bugs are harmless.

exercises.prompt: What does a good forest ranger do with insects?
options: Watches them, respects them and stays safe without wiping them out
exercises.explanation: Watch, respect and stay safe: that's the secret.

exam.title: Unit challenge
exam.intro: Final challenge! Pass it and you finish Hexa, and you can tell Paquito how you feel about insects now.
exam.closing: Congratulations, forest ranger! Now you know almost all insects are friends, and how to stay safe from the few that can sting.

exercises.prompt: Match each insect with its job.
exercises.explanation: Pollinating, controlling pests and recycling.

exercises.prompt: What is a pest?
options: Huge numbers of one kind of insect that damage crops or food
exercises.explanation: A pest outbreak is when there are huge numbers of one kind of insect damaging crops or food. One insect alone isn't a pest outbreak.

exercises.prompt: What is biological control?
options: Using the pest's natural enemies, like ladybugs against aphids
exercises.explanation: Using their natural enemies, like the ladybug that eats aphids, without poison that harms bees.

exercises.prompt: Where do mosquitoes lay their eggs?
options: In still water: buckets, tires or vases
exercises.explanation: In still water.

exercises.prompt: Put each insect in its box.
bins: Careful: can sting or spread disease
exercises.explanation: Harmless ones, pests and the ones that can bite.

exercises.prompt: What helps stop mosquitoes from hatching near your home?
exercises.explanation: Emptying still water: that's where mosquitoes lay their eggs. Without standing water, they can't hatch.

exercises.prompt: If we spray insecticide all over the garden, what happens?
options: Bees, ladybugs and other helpers die too
exercises.explanation: The helpers die too.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: For there to be fruit, insects ___ the flowers.
exercises.explanation: Bees, butterflies and many other insects carry pollen from flower to flower, and that's how plants make fruit.

exercises.prompt: A bee stings you and it swells up a lot or it's hard to breathe. What do you do?
options: I tell an adult right away
exercises.explanation: Tell an adult right away: if it swells a lot or it's hard to breathe, you need to see a doctor.

exercises.prompt: What does a good forest ranger do with insects?
options: Watches them, respects them and stays safe without wiping them out
exercises.explanation: Watch, respect and stay safe.
